title: JESUS DIDN’T SAY BEAUTY WAS SIN—So What Exactly Is “LUST”?
paragraphs: JESUS DIDN’T SAY BEAUTY WAS SIN—So What Exactly Is “LUST”?

Matthew 5:28 may be one of the most quoted teachings of Jesus about sexual purity—and one of the easiest to flatten into something Jesus was not actually saying. Because there is a difference between seeing someone beautiful…and choosing to turn that person into an object inside your heart.
Maybe nobody ever explained that difference to you.
Maybe you were taught that if your eyes noticed an attractive person, you had already sinned.
So you became afraid of your own eyes.
Afraid of attraction.
Afraid of beauty.
Afraid that one involuntary moment of noticing another human being meant you had already committed adultery before God.
And perhaps that fear created something even worse.
You began hiding.
You learned how to smile at church while carrying secret shame.
You learned how to worship with raised hands while wondering whether God was disgusted with what was happening inside your head.
Or maybe your story went in the opposite direction.
Maybe you stopped fighting altogether.
You told yourself everybody looks.
Everybody fantasizes.
Everybody scrolls.
Everybody secretly wants things they should not have.
And somewhere between shame and normalization, the words of Jesus became blurred.
But what if we actually listened to what Jesus said?
Not what pornography culture says.
Not what shame culture says.
Not what social media says.
Not what religious fear says.
Jesus.
Because His words are stronger than our excuses…
but they are also more precise than our shame.
Matthew 5:27–28 records Jesus saying:
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
And underneath that English translation sits something worth seeing.
The Greek reads:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn
The crucial expression is:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι — pros to epithymēsai
It carries the idea of looking toward, or for the purpose of, desiring.
That matters.
Jesus does not say that the human eye becomes sinful simply because it recognizes beauty.
He is confronting something deeper.
The look that becomes intentional.
The gaze that is entertained.
The desire that is cultivated.
The moment another human being stops being someone made in the image of God and becomes material for private consumption.
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because lust is not merely about what your eyes accidentally encounter.
It is about what your heart chooses to do with what your eyes have seen.
There is a difference between noticing and nurturing.
Between attraction and possession.
Between temptation arriving at your door and inviting it inside, giving it a chair, feeding it, replaying it, and asking it to stay.
And Jesus goes directly to that hidden room.
He does not merely ask, “What did your body do?”
He asks what your heart wanted to do.
That was devastating in a culture where a person could congratulate himself for technically avoiding physical adultery while privately cultivating adulterous desire.
Jesus takes the commandment deeper than external compliance.
“You shall not commit adultery” was already God’s command.
Jesus does not weaken it.
He exposes its roots.
Before adultery becomes a bed, it can become a fantasy.
Before betrayal reaches the hands, it can be welcomed by the heart.
Before certain sins become visible scandals, they have often been rehearsed privately where nobody but God can see them.
And that means some of the most dangerous spiritual battles of your life may happen in places nobody applauds you for winning.
Your bedroom.
Your phone.
Your browser.
Your imagination.
That second look.
That private message.
That profile you keep revisiting.
That fantasy you keep feeding.
That relationship you keep emotionally crossing boundaries with while insisting, “Nothing actually happened.”
Jesus cares about what happens there.
Not because beauty is evil.
God created beauty.
Not because sexuality itself is dirty.
God created human beings as embodied creatures and established marriage before humanity's fall into sin.
The problem is not that another human being can be beautiful.
The problem begins when desire refuses to honor the person.
Lust says:
I want your body without responsibility for your soul.
I want pleasure without covenant.
I want intimacy without faithfulness.
I want the image of God in you reduced to something that exists for me.
Love moves differently.
Love can recognize beauty without demanding ownership.
Love can experience attraction without making attraction its master.
Love asks what honors God and what protects the other person.
Lust asks what can satisfy me.
And suddenly Matthew 5:28 is no longer merely a verse about “looking.”
It is about worship.
Who gets to command your desires?
That is why Jesus’ next words are so severe.
He speaks about tearing out the right eye if it causes you to stumble and cutting off the right hand if it causes you to stumble.

Jesus is using shocking language to communicate the seriousness with which sin must be confronted. The point is not that physical mutilation can purify a sinful heart. Removing an eye cannot remove desire from the soul.
The point is that sin is not something to negotiate with.
There are things you may need to remove.
Not your literal eye.
Maybe the account.
Maybe the app.
Maybe the private conversation.
Maybe the secret folder.
Maybe the late-night scrolling.
Maybe the relationship whose boundaries you keep pretending are harmless.
Maybe the device should stop sleeping beside you.
Maybe accountability needs to become more than something Christians talk about.
Maybe repentance needs to cost you convenience.
Because we sometimes pray,
“Jesus, make me pure,”
while protecting the exact doorway through which impurity keeps entering.
And then we wonder why the battle never changes.
But there is another danger here.
Please don't miss this.
You can read Matthew 5:28 and become so obsessed with your failure that you forget who is speaking.
Jesus.
The One who exposes the heart is also the One who came to save sinners.
The Sermon on the Mount is not permission to minimize sin.
But neither is Christianity an invitation to spend the rest of your life drowning in self-hatred.
Jesus does something far greater.
He brings darkness into the light so darkness does not have to own you anymore.
Perhaps you have failed here.
Not once.
Hundreds of times.
Perhaps pornography became a secret refuge.
Perhaps fantasy became the place you escaped whenever loneliness became unbearable.
Perhaps you crossed emotional boundaries with somebody who was not your spouse.
Perhaps you have objectified people while publicly presenting yourself as spiritually mature.
Perhaps nobody knows.
And perhaps reading this has made your stomach tighten because you know exactly what God has been putting His finger on.
Don't run.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
The same Bible that refuses to rename sin also refuses to tell repentant sinners that their sin is beyond the reach of Christ.
The answer to lust is not pretending it isn't serious.
The answer is not learning to hate yourself.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
At the cross, Jesus did not die for the cleaned-up version of you that you hope eventually exists.
Christ died for sinners.
Real sinners.
People with histories.
People with secret tabs.
People with memories they wish they could erase.
People who have betrayed.
People who have fantasized.
People who have been sexually broken.
People who have used others.
People who have themselves been used.
People whose hearts desperately need cleansing.
And Scripture gives us this astonishing promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not excuse.
Forgive.
Not redefine.
Cleanse.
Not pretend the wound never existed.
Redeem.
That is the difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation whispers:
“Hide from God because of what you did.”
The Gospel calls:
“Bring what you did to Christ.”
Condemnation says:
“You are filthy, so stay away.”
Grace says:
“You cannot cleanse yourself. Come to the One who can.”
Repentance is therefore not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Biblical repentance turns.
It brings sin into the light.
It stops protecting what Jesus is asking us to surrender.
And sometimes repentance sounds less dramatic than we expect.
“Jesus, I have been feeding this.”
“I have been pretending this wasn't serious.”
“I have been blaming everybody except myself.”
“I have looked at people as bodies instead of souls.”
“I have entertained desires I should have surrendered.”
“Lord, forgive me.”
There is no performance required in that prayer.
No theatrical Christianity.
Just truth.
Because the most terrifying thing about hidden sin is not simply that somebody might eventually discover it.
It is that you can become comfortable hiding something from the God who already sees it.
But the most beautiful thing about grace is this:
God already knows the thing you are terrified to confess…
and still calls you to come.
Maybe this article is not really about somebody else's lust.
Maybe it is about yours.
Maybe this is the moment the excuses stop.
Maybe tonight you stop deleting history only from your browser and start bringing your history to Jesus.
Maybe you finally tell somebody trustworthy that you need help.
Maybe you install accountability.
Maybe you end the conversation.
Maybe you unfollow the account.
Maybe you confess to your spouse.
Maybe you stop calling bondage “just a weakness.”
Not because those actions purchase forgiveness.
Jesus already paid what you could never pay.
You take sin seriously because grace has made freedom possible.
And if you fall again?
Do not make peace with the fall.
Get up.
Confess.
Repent.
Run toward Christ again.
Fight again.
There is a difference between struggling against sin and surrendering yourself to it.
A wounded soldier is still a soldier.
So fight.
Not to convince Jesus to love you.
Fight because in Christ you have discovered a love worth becoming free for.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years believing that simply finding another person attractive made them filthy.
Hear this carefully.
Beauty is not the enemy.
Another person's body is not the enemy.
Women are not the enemy.
Men are not the enemy.
Your body is not the enemy.
The battle is over whether desire will remain under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
You can notice beauty and choose honor.
You can experience temptation and choose obedience.
You can feel desire without allowing desire to become your god.
And when you fail, you can repent instead of hiding.
That is freedom.
Not the absence of temptation.
The presence of a greater King.
Jesus.
So the next time your eyes notice somebody beautiful, perhaps the question should not merely be:
“Did I see?”
Ask:
“What am I choosing to do with what I saw?”
Am I honoring this person as somebody created in God's image?
Or am I mentally taking something that was never mine?
Am I letting attraction pass through open hands?
Or am I turning it into fantasy?
Am I looking…
or am I feeding?
That question may expose you.
Good.
Because whatever Jesus exposes, He calls us to bring into His light.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail of your private struggle.
But you also do not have to pretend.
There may be another believer reading the comments tonight who desperately needs to discover that they are not the only person fighting for purity.
And if you know somebody trapped between lust and shame, share this with them.
Not to expose them.
Not to embarrass them.
Send it because you love them enough to remind them that Jesus offers something stronger than secrecy.

Supporting Gospel ministry financially should never be treated as purchasing God's favor, forgiveness, blessing, or salvation. Giving in the New Testament is to be willing rather than coerced—“not reluctantly or under compulsion,” as Paul teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7.
But voluntary generosity can genuinely help Gospel work continue.

If you want to glorify God with your resources, supporting faithful Christian ministry can be one way—among many—to practice generosity and help put biblical teaching before people who desperately need Jesus.
And whether or not you are able to give financially, you can still help.
Because this was never supposed to end with an argument about what technically qualifies as lust.
It should end with a heart standing naked before Jesus and asking:
“Lord, what have I allowed myself to desire that I need to surrender to You?”
And maybe that is the question you have been avoiding.
The scandal may be what happened inside your heart where nobody could see it.
But Jesus sees deeper than the scandal.
He sees the sinner He came to redeem.
So stop hiding.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the years you cannot undo.
Bring Him the heart you cannot cleanse by yourself.
Repent.
Receive His grace.
Then get up and walk differently.
Because the final word over a repentant sinner does not belong to lust.
It does not belong to shame.
It does not belong to your browser history.
It does not belong to your worst night.
The sin you are terrified will become the final sentence of your story may become the very place where Jesus teaches you what redemption means.
